editorial.headline: The Unseen Work Behind a Live Performance
editorial.standfirst: This activity gathers the producing, technical, artistic and critical work that makes live arts happen—and reveals a sharp divide between national openness and Bali registration.
editorial.body:
A live performance is never only the person in the spotlight. This activity covers the supporting work involved in producing and staging live arts and stage entertainment: drama and theatre, music performances and concerts, opera, plays, pantomime, dance, regional arts performances, bands and orchestras. It describes the operational and creative framework that lets a performance move from an idea to a functioning event.

Its cast of professionals is broad. Producers, stage managers and arts managers sit alongside stage-set designers, scenographers and stage visual artists; scene-shifters, lighting engineers and sound-system specialists carry the practical work of presentation. The scope also includes directors, dramaturgs, artistic directors, film promoters, programme makers and supervisors, as well as curators and literary or visual-art critics. It is therefore an activity for those whose work shapes, organises, presents, interprets or supports an artistic programme, rather than only those appearing before an audience.

The record opens this activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. At the national level, PMA is classified as TERBUKA and permits foreign ownership up to 100%. In plain terms, the national record does not set the foreign stake below full ownership for this activity. That is an important part of the picture, but it is not the whole of it: national openness does not itself determine whether a PMA registration can proceed in Bali.

In Bali, the position is decisive: a PMA investor cannot register this activity there today. At the Besar scale, the OSS risk classification is Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every scope, bringing the activity within Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium on PMA registrations for all Low and Medium-Low-risk KBLI. The result is a Bali-specific registration block, not a reduction of the national 100% foreign-ownership ceiling. For founders, the distinction matters precisely because both statements are true at once: the activity is nationally open to PMA, yet blocked for PMA registration in Bali under the stated moratorium.
editorial.pullQuote: National openness and a Bali PMA registration block can both be true for the same activity.
